js-advanced:0.explanation: for...of logs 0, then gets 1 and hits break. Leaving the loop early calls the iterator's optional return() method, so 'cleanup' prints. return() is not called when the loop finishes normally, only on early exit (break, return, throw).

An iterator is single-pass. The first spread drains it; the second spread calls next() on an exhausted iterator, which returns done: true at once, giving an empty array. The array itself is re-iterable because each for...of or spread asks it for a fresh iterator.

Array destructuring pulls only as many values as it needs: one next() call runs the body up to the first yield ('start'). Because the iterator isn't done, destructuring then calls return(), which finishes the generator without running 'mid' or 'end'.

js-advanced:0.prompt: What makes a plain object usable in a for...of loop?
options: Defining a [Symbol.iterator]() method that returns an object with a next() method
Defining a next() method directly on the object that returns { value, done }
Giving the object a numeric length property and integer keys starting at 0
Defining a [Symbol.asyncIterator]() method that returns an object with next()
js-advanced:0.explanation: for...of calls obj[Symbol.iterator]() to get an iterator, then calls next() until done is true. An object that only has next() is an iterator but not an iterable. Array-likes with length are not iterable, and Symbol.asyncIterator is only used by for await...of.

js-advanced:0.prompt: Why is for...of preferred over for...in for walking the elements of an array?
options: for...in skips index 0 of an array, because the key 0 is falsy and the loop treats it as a stop signal
for...of is the only loop that works on arrays created with new Array(), which have no own keys yet
for...in can't be used on arrays at all; it throws a TypeError because arrays aren't plain objects
for...in visits enumerable string keys (including inherited ones), not the element values
js-advanced:0.explanation: for...in enumerates property keys as strings, including enumerable inherited properties (e.g. something added to Array.prototype). for...of uses the array's iterator and yields values in order. for...in does work on arrays; it just iterates the wrong thing.

js-advanced:0.prompt: A paginated REST client should let callers process items one at a time and stop early without fetching the remaining pages. Which design fits best?
options: A synchronous iterator whose next() starts every page request and returns a Promise for each page
An EventEmitter that emits an 'item' event for every result as fast as the pages arrive from the API
An async generator (Symbol.asyncIterator) that fetches the next page only when the consumer asks for more
A method that fetches every page up front in parallel and resolves a Promise with one combined array
js-advanced:0.explanation: An async iterator is pull-based: the next page is only requested when the for await...of loop asks for more, and break triggers return() so no further fetches happen. Fetching everything up front wastes requests and memory; an emitter pushes data with no back-pressure.

js-advanced:0.prompt: Why does map.keys()[0] evaluate to undefined for a non-empty Map?
options: Map keys can only be read back with map.get() or map.has(), never enumerated
map.keys() returns an iterator object, not an array, so it has no index properties
Map keys are stored in hash order, so there's no stable index 0 to return
map.keys() returns a Promise of the key list that has to be awaited first
js-advanced:0.explanation: keys(), values() and entries() return Map iterator objects. They are iterable but are not arrays, so there's no [0] property. Use [...map.keys()][0] or map.keys().next().value. Maps actually keep keys in insertion order, so ordering isn't the problem.

js-advanced:0.prompt: Which of these are iterable by default (usable with for...of)? Select all that apply.
options: The arguments object inside a regular function
A string
A plain object literal { a: 1 }
A Set
A WeakMap
js-advanced:0.explanation: Strings (by code point), Set, Map, arrays, typed arrays and arguments implement Symbol.iterator. Plain objects don't (use Object.entries). WeakMap isn't iterable because its keys can be garbage-collected at any time.

js-advanced:0.prompt: Which of these consume their argument through the iterable protocol (Symbol.iterator)? Select all that apply.
options: Spread into an array literal: [...x]
Promise.all(x)
Object.keys(x)
Array destructuring: const [a] = x
JSON.stringify(x)
js-advanced:0.explanation: Spread, array destructuring, Promise.all/allSettled/race/any, Array.from, new Map/Set and for...of all use Symbol.iterator. Object.keys reads own enumerable properties and JSON.stringify serialises properties; neither calls the iterator, which is why a Map stringifies to {}.

js-advanced:0.prompt: If a hand-written iterator never returns done: true, spreading it with [...it] will never finish (it loops until memory runs out).
options: True
False
js-advanced:0.explanation: Spread keeps calling next() until done is true, collecting values into an array. An infinite iterator is fine with for...of plus break, or with destructuring that takes a fixed number of items, but spread and Array.from try to drain it completely.

js-advanced:0.prompt: Every iterator is also an iterable.
options: True
False
js-advanced:0.explanation: Built-in iterators (and generator objects) are iterable because their [Symbol.iterator]() returns this. A hand-written object that only has next() is an iterator but not an iterable, so for...of over it throws 'is not iterable' unless you also add [Symbol.iterator]() { return this; }.

js-advanced:1.explanation: The value passed to next() becomes the result of the yield the generator is paused at. The first next() starts the body, so there's no paused yield and 'ignored' is discarded. The second next(5) resumes yield 1 with 5, logs 'got 5', then yields 10.

A generator's return value is delivered with done: true. Spread and for...of stop as soon as done is true and ignore that value, so the array is [1, 2]. Calling next() manually a third time shows { value: 3, done: true }.

return(9) resumes the paused generator as if a return statement ran at the yield. The finally block runs first (logging 'finally'), then the generator completes with { value: 9, done: true }. This is how for...of with break lets generators release resources.

yield* re-yields every value from inner ('a'), and the expression evaluates to inner's return value ('r'), which outer then yields itself. The return value of the delegate isn't yielded automatically, which is why the output isn't 'a r r'.

js-advanced:1.prompt: What happens when you call a generator function g()?
options: It runs the whole body immediately and returns an array of every value that was yielded
It returns a Promise that resolves with the return value once the generator body finishes
It returns a suspended generator object; the body starts running on the first next() call
It runs the body up to the first yield, pauses there, and returns the first yielded value
js-advanced:1.explanation: Calling a generator function runs none of its body. It creates a generator object in the suspended-start state; each next() runs until the following yield. Running to the first yield on call is a common misconception.

js-advanced:1.prompt: An async generator streams rows from a database cursor and a for await...of loop processes each row slowly. What happens to the producer while the consumer is busy?
options: It drops any rows the consumer hasn't processed yet and resumes from the newest one later
It stays paused at its yield and does not fetch more rows until the loop asks for the next one
It keeps fetching rows in the background and buffers all of them in memory until they're read
It throws a back-pressure error once more than 16 unread rows are waiting in its internal queue
js-advanced:1.explanation: Async generators are pull-based. After yielding, the generator is suspended until the consumer calls next() again (which for await does only after the loop body finishes). That gives natural back-pressure, unlike push-based emitters that keep producing.

js-advanced:1.prompt: Inside async function main(), a for await...of loop iterates an async generator that throws on its third item. What happens?
options: The error is thrown from the for await statement and can be caught by a try/catch around the loop in main()
The loop silently skips the failed item and continues with the next one
The error becomes an uncaught exception that crashes the process even if the loop is wrapped in try/catch
The loop finishes normally and the error is stored on the generator's .error property
js-advanced:1.explanation: A rejected next() promise is surfaced at the for await statement, just like a rejected await. A surrounding try/catch in the async function handles it; if nothing catches it, main()'s promise rejects. Nothing is skipped or stored.

js-advanced:1.prompt: Which statements about async generators (async function*) are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Array.from(asyncGen()) returns an array of the resolved values
Their next() returns a Promise of { value, done }
They can be consumed with for await...of
They can be consumed with a plain for...of loop
Their body may use both await and yield
js-advanced:1.explanation: Async generators implement Symbol.asyncIterator, not Symbol.iterator, so a plain for...of throws 'is not iterable' and Array.from doesn't see them as iterable (Array.fromAsync is the async counterpart). Inside, you can await and yield freely.

js-advanced:1.prompt: Which are good uses for generators in a Node.js backend? Select all that apply.
options: Running CPU-heavy work in parallel on multiple cores
Implementing [Symbol.iterator] for a custom collection in a few lines
Producing a lazy, potentially infinite sequence such as ID or backoff-delay values
Streaming paginated API or DB results one item at a time with an async generator
js-advanced:1.explanation: Generators give you lazy evaluation and a compact way to write iterators. They still run on the same thread: yielding doesn't create parallelism, so CPU-heavy work needs worker_threads or a separate process.

js-advanced:1.prompt: Calling next() on a generator that has already completed returns { value: undefined, done: true } instead of throwing.
options: True
False
js-advanced:1.explanation: Once a generator has finished (returned or thrown), any further next() calls return { value: undefined, done: true }. That's why iterating an exhausted generator a second time just produces nothing.

js-advanced:1.prompt: Rewriting a long CPU-bound loop as a generator moves the work to another thread, so the event loop stays responsive.
options: True
False
js-advanced:1.explanation: Generators only pause and resume on the same thread. Each next() call runs synchronously until the next yield. You could yield and schedule chunks with setImmediate to give the event loop room, but real parallelism needs worker_threads.

js-advanced:2.prompt: An ES module running on Node 22 uses __dirname and crashes with a ReferenceError. What's the idiomatic fix?
options: Rename the file to .mts so Node injects the CommonJS wrapper variables
Use import.meta.dirname (or derive the path from import.meta.url with fileURLToPath)
Add 'use strict' at the top of the file so the CommonJS globals are defined
Import __dirname from the node:path module
js-advanced:2.explanation: __dirname, __filename, require and module come from the CommonJS module wrapper, which ES modules don't have. Node 20.11+ provides import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename; on older versions use path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)). node:path doesn't export __dirname.

js-advanced:2.prompt: counter.mjs exports a live counter. What does main.mjs print?
options: undefined
TypeError: Assignment to constant variable
js-advanced:2.explanation: ES module imports are live bindings to the exporter's variable, not copies. After inc() updates count inside counter.mjs, main sees 1. With CommonJS, destructuring module.exports would copy the value 0 at require time, which is the usual trap.

js-advanced:2.prompt: On a recent Node version where require() can load ES modules (Node 22.12+ / 24), a CommonJS file calls require('./setup.mjs'), and setup.mjs uses top-level await. What happens?
options: require() blocks the thread until the top-level await settles, then returns the namespace
require() returns a Promise of the module namespace
require() returns the namespace immediately, with exports still undefined until the await finishes
require() throws (ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE); use dynamic import() instead
js-advanced:2.explanation: require() is synchronous, so it can only load an ES module whose graph evaluates synchronously. If the module (or one of its dependencies) uses top-level await, Node throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE. await import() handles async module graphs.

js-advanced:2.prompt: config.mjs uses top-level await to fetch secrets before exporting them. app.mjs imports config.mjs. How does this affect app.mjs?
options: Top-level await is only allowed in the entry module, so config.mjs fails to parse at startup
app.mjs must switch to await import('./config.mjs'), because a static import won't wait for it
app.mjs's body doesn't run until config.mjs's awaited promise settles; if it rejects, app.mjs fails to load
app.mjs runs right away and sees undefined exports from config.mjs until the secrets arrive
js-advanced:2.explanation: Top-level await makes a module's evaluation asynchronous, and modules that import it wait for it to finish before their own bodies run. A rejection propagates and the importing graph fails. It's handy for one-off initialisation but delays startup and should not be used for slow, optional work.

js-advanced:2.prompt: Why can bundlers tree-shake ES modules much more reliably than CommonJS?
options: ES modules are loaded lazily, so exports nobody imports are never downloaded at all
import/export are static, so the used exports are known without running any code
ES modules are compiled to bytecode ahead of time, so unused code is already stripped
CommonJS modules can't export functions, only plain objects, which can't be split
js-advanced:2.explanation: ESM imports and exports must appear at the top level with literal specifiers, so tools can analyse them statically. require() is an ordinary function call that can be conditional, computed, or mutate module.exports at runtime, which blocks safe dead-code removal.

js-advanced:2.prompt: Your package.json has "type": "module", but a tool needs one config file written in CommonJS (module.exports = ...). What's the simplest fix?
options: Give that file the .cjs extension
Add 'use commonjs' at the top of the file
Remove "type": "module" and rename every other file to .mjs
Wrap the file's contents in an async IIFE
js-advanced:2.explanation: The .cjs extension always means CommonJS and .mjs always means ESM, whatever the nearest package.json "type" says. There's no 'use commonjs' directive, and flipping the whole package for one file is unnecessary churn.

js-advanced:2.prompt: In CommonJS, a.js requires b.js and b.js requires a.js. b.js reads a.helper at load time and gets undefined, although a.js defines module.exports.helper. Why?
options: CommonJS doesn't support circular requires and always returns undefined for the second one
require caches modules by file size, so the cached copy of a.js is stale
helper is hoisted to the top of a.js only when it's declared with var
b.js receives a's exports object while a.js is still running, before helper has been assigned
js-advanced:2.explanation: When a cycle is hit, Node returns the partially built module.exports of the module that's still executing. Anything a.js assigns after its require('./b') line isn't there yet. Fixes: move the shared code into a third module, or read a.helper lazily inside a function.

js-advanced:2.prompt: In a Node ES module, import { db } from './db' fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND even though db.js exists next to it. What's wrong?
options: Named imports require the exporting file to be renamed to .mjs
The import must be written as require('./db') inside an ES module
Relative ESM imports in Node need the full file extension: './db.js'
ES modules can only import from node_modules, not relative paths
js-advanced:2.explanation: Node's ESM resolver doesn't guess extensions or index files the way require() does. Relative specifiers must be exact ('./db.js', './lib/index.js'). TypeScript with module/moduleResolution set to nodenext enforces the same rule.

js-advanced:2.prompt: Which statements about ES modules vs CommonJS in Node are correct? Select all that apply.
options: require() returns a Promise of the module
Static imports are resolved and evaluated before the importing module's body runs
require() can be called conditionally, e.g. inside an if block
Top-level `this` is undefined in an ES module
Named imports from any CommonJS module work for every property it sets at runtime
js-advanced:2.explanation: Static imports are hoisted and the dependency graph is evaluated first. require() is a normal synchronous function call. In ESM top-level this is undefined (in CJS it's module.exports). Named imports from CJS only work for exports Node can detect statically; the default import (module.exports) always works.

js-advanced:2.prompt: Which statements about dynamic import() are correct? Select all that apply.
options: It returns a Promise that resolves to the module namespace object
It can be used inside CommonJS files
The specifier can be computed at runtime
It's synchronous, like require()
It's only allowed at the top level of a module
js-advanced:2.explanation: import() is an expression that works in both module systems, accepts a runtime-computed string and returns a Promise, which makes it the standard way to load ESM-only packages from CJS or to lazy-load code. It can appear anywhere an expression can, inside functions and conditionals.

js-advanced:2.prompt: In an ES module, after import x from './a.js', the importer can reassign x = 5 because it holds its own copy of a's default export.
options: True
False
js-advanced:2.explanation: Imported bindings are read-only views of the exporter's binding. Assigning to x throws a TypeError (Assignment to constant variable). Only the exporting module can change the value, and importers see the change because the binding is live.

js-advanced:3.explanation: The inner catch wraps the JSON SyntaxError in a new Error with the options bag { cause }. The outer handler sees the wrapper's message, and e.cause still points at the original SyntaxError with its own name and stack.

distractors: true true Error: bad email email
false true ValidationError: bad email email
true false ValidationError: bad email email
js-advanced:3.explanation: class extends Error sets up the prototype chain correctly, so both instanceof checks are true. Error.prototype.toString uses this.name, which the constructor overrode, giving 'ValidationError: bad email'. Without that assignment it would print 'Error: bad email'.

throw accepts any value. Throwing a string gives you the string itself, with no stack trace or name. That's why code should always throw Error objects, and why TypeScript types catch variables as unknown.

Promise.any resolves with the first fulfilment. If every input rejects it rejects with an AggregateError whose errors array holds all the rejection reasons in input order. It doesn't reject with just the first or last error.

js-advanced:3.prompt: An HTTP API needs to turn domain failures (not found, conflict, validation) into the right status codes. Which approach is most robust?
options: Check err.message for phrases like 'not found' or 'already exists' in the error handler
Return null from services on any failure and let each controller decide which status fits
Catch every error inside each route handler and always respond with a 500 and the message
Throw custom error classes carrying a status or code, and map them in one central handler
js-advanced:3.explanation: Typed errors (instanceof checks, or a stable code field) give one place that maps failures to responses, and messages can change freely. Matching on message text breaks on rewording or translation, and returning null throws away the reason.

js-advanced:3.prompt: Production logs show 'ReferenceError: user is not defined'. What's the most likely cause?
options: JSON.parse was given an invalid string while deserialising the user from the session store
A recursive function that loads the user exceeded the maximum call stack size
Code reads an identifier that isn't declared in scope, or a let/const before its declaration
Code reads a property such as user.id on a variable whose value is currently undefined
js-advanced:3.explanation: ReferenceError means name resolution failed: an undeclared identifier, a typo, or a let/const accessed in its temporal dead zone. Reading a property of undefined is a TypeError, invalid JSON gives a SyntaxError, and stack overflow is a RangeError.

js-advanced:3.prompt: Why wrap a low-level error with new Error('Failed to charge card', { cause: err }) instead of building a new message by concatenating err.message?
options: V8 truncates error messages to 100 characters, so concatenated messages lose the original
cause keeps the original error object (type, stack, code) available for logs and checks
cause makes the outer error catchable by try/catch blocks that would otherwise miss it
cause makes Node retry the failed operation once automatically before the error is thrown
js-advanced:3.explanation: With cause you add context while keeping the full original error: its stack shows where the failure really began, and its code (e.g. ECONNRESET) can still be inspected. cause doesn't change how the error is caught; any thrown value can be caught.

js-advanced:3.prompt: Many Node APIs and libraries expose err.code (e.g. 'ECONNREFUSED', 'ERR_INVALID_ARG_TYPE') and recommend checking it rather than err.message or instanceof. Why?
options: Codes are a stable contract; messages get reworded and instanceof can fail across realms
err.code is the only Error property that survives JSON serialisation between services
instanceof doesn't work on Error subclasses when the code runs in strict mode
Node only fills in err.message when NODE_ENV is set to 'development', not in production
js-advanced:3.explanation: Messages are for humans and get reworded. instanceof compares prototype identity, which breaks when an error comes from another vm context or worker, or when two copies of a library are installed. A documented string code is the stable thing to branch on.

js-advanced:3.prompt: Which statements about JavaScript errors are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Passing { cause } as the second Error constructor argument sets err.cause
throw accepts any value, not only Error instances
catch {} without a binding is valid syntax
Subclassing Error with class extends loses the stack trace
A Promise can only be rejected with an Error instance
js-advanced:3.explanation: ES2022 added the { cause } option, and optional catch binding (catch {}) has been valid since ES2019. Subclassing with class extends keeps a proper stack. Promises can be rejected with any value, which is why rejection reasons should be treated as unknown.

js-advanced:3.prompt: Which of these are operational errors (expected failures to handle gracefully) rather than programmer errors (bugs to fix)? Select all that apply.
options: A request body that fails validation
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined in your own handler
A timeout calling a downstream service
Calling an internal function with arguments in the wrong order
ECONNRESET from the database connection
js-advanced:3.explanation: Operational errors come from the environment or inputs (network, timeouts, bad user data) and should be retried, reported or turned into 4xx/5xx responses. TypeErrors from your own code and wrong internal calls are bugs: log them, fix them, and don't try to recover in place.

js-advanced:3.prompt: An error thrown inside a setTimeout callback is caught by a try/catch that wraps the setTimeout() call.
options: True
False
js-advanced:3.explanation: setTimeout returns immediately; the callback runs later on a fresh call stack after the try block has already exited. The error becomes an uncaught exception. Put the try/catch inside the callback, or use promises with await.

js-advanced:4.explanation: There's no set trap, so p.a = 1 is forwarded to the target. The get trap then finds 'a' on the target and returns 1, and returns a fallback string for the missing key 'b'. Any operation without a trap is forwarded to the target unchanged.

When a set trap returns false, assignment in strict mode throws a TypeError (in sloppy mode it fails silently). y is never written. Object.keys has no ownKeys trap to intercept it, so it reads the target's keys, which only include 'x'.
The has trap intercepts the in operator. The key arrives as the string '5', and Number('5') is in range. Number('a') is NaN, and every comparison with NaN is false, so 'a' in range is false.

js-advanced:4.prompt: Why do get traps usually call Reflect.get(target, key, receiver) rather than return target[key]?
options: target[key] returns a shallow copy of object values instead of the original reference
Passing receiver keeps `this` correct for getters, including when the proxy is a prototype
target[key] would recursively trigger the same get trap again and overflow the call stack
Reflect.get is the only way to read symbol-keyed properties from inside a proxy handler
js-advanced:4.explanation: If the property is a getter, target[key] runs it with this === target, which skips the proxy (and any traps on the properties the getter reads) and breaks inheritance through the proxy. Reflect.get with receiver forwards the right this. Reading target directly doesn't recurse, because target isn't the proxy.

js-advanced:4.prompt: A proxy wraps a frozen object, and its get trap returns a different value for one of the frozen properties. What happens when that property is read?
options: A TypeError is thrown, because the trap breaks an invariant of frozen properties
The trap's value is returned, because traps always take precedence over the target
The original value is returned and the trap's result is silently ignored
The proxy unfreezes the target so that the two values become consistent again
js-advanced:4.explanation: Proxies enforce invariants: for a non-configurable, non-writable data property, get must report the real value. Breaking that throws a TypeError. Invariants stop proxies from lying about guarantees like Object.freeze.

js-advanced:4.prompt: Vue 3 switched from Object.defineProperty getters/setters to Proxy for reactivity. What's the main capability this added?
options: It makes reactive property reads faster than reads on plain objects
It lets reactive state be shared safely across worker threads
It deep-clones the state automatically on every write, preventing mutation bugs
It detects properties added or deleted after creation, and array index changes
js-advanced:4.explanation: defineProperty can only intercept properties that already exist, so new keys, delete and some array mutations needed special APIs. A Proxy intercepts get/set/deleteProperty/has for any key. It's actually slower than plain property access, not faster.

js-advanced:4.prompt: A team wraps every database row object in a Proxy to log property reads, and p99 latency on a hot endpoint rises noticeably. What's the most likely reason?
options: Proxies force each wrapped object onto the old-generation heap, so GC runs more often
console.log inside a trap always performs synchronous disk I/O on every single call
Every property read now calls a trap function, bypassing V8's inline-cache fast paths
Proxies copy the whole target object on every property read to keep the target safe
js-advanced:4.explanation: A property read on a plain object can be a single optimised load once inline caches warm up. On a proxy, every read calls a JavaScript function through the handler, which is far slower. Keep proxies off hot paths, or log at a coarser level.

js-advanced:4.prompt: What does Proxy.revocable() give you that new Proxy() doesn't?
options: A proxy that only allows reads, with no extra handler code
A revoke() function; after calling it, every operation on the proxy throws a TypeError
A proxy that automatically reverts the target's changes when it's garbage-collected
A proxy whose traps can be swapped at runtime
js-advanced:4.explanation: Proxy.revocable returns { proxy, revoke }. Once revoked, the proxy drops its target and handler and any trap-able operation throws. That's useful for handing out temporary access to an object, for example to plugin code.

js-advanced:4.prompt: Which operations can a Proxy handler intercept? Select all that apply.
options: delete obj.prop (deleteProperty)
Calling the proxy as a function, if its target is a function (apply)
The result of typeof proxy
Strict equality proxy === other
Reading a property (get)
The in operator (has)
js-advanced:4.explanation: There are 13 traps, including get, set, has, deleteProperty, ownKeys, apply and construct. typeof just reflects the target (function or object), and === compares identity, so neither can be trapped.

js-advanced:4.prompt: Which statements about Reflect are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Reflect.has(obj, key) behaves like key in obj
Reflect methods only work when the target is a Proxy
Reflect.ownKeys(obj) returns both string and symbol own keys, including non-enumerable ones
Reflect.defineProperty returns false on failure instead of throwing like Object.defineProperty
new Reflect() creates a reflection wrapper around an object
js-advanced:4.explanation: Reflect is a plain namespace object (not a constructor) whose methods mirror the proxy traps and work on any object. They give the default behaviour as a function, with boolean results where Object.* would throw, which makes them the natural way to forward from a trap.

js-advanced:4.prompt: A proxy and its target are the same object, so proxy === target is true.
options: True
False
js-advanced:4.explanation: new Proxy(target, handler) creates a separate exotic object. proxy === target is false, which matters when objects are used as Map/WeakMap keys or compared by identity. Code holding the raw target also bypasses every trap.

js-advanced:5.prompt: A Node service's memory climbs for hours until it's restarted. What's the most effective first step to find what's retaining memory?
options: Start node with --expose-gc and call global.gc() at the end of every request handler
Rewrite the hot paths to use var instead of let so fewer block scopes are allocated
Take two heap snapshots some time apart and compare which objects grew and what retains them
Raise --max-old-space-size step by step until the restarts stop happening in production
js-advanced:5.explanation: Comparing heap snapshots (Chrome DevTools or --heapsnapshot-signal) shows which constructors keep growing, and the retainers view shows the reference chain keeping them alive, often a module-level Map, a listener array or a closure. A bigger heap only delays the crash.

js-advanced:5.prompt: Two objects reference each other, and nothing else references either of them. What does V8's garbage collector do?
options: Throws a RangeError for a circular structure
Collects both, because neither is reachable from a root
Keeps both forever, because their reference counts never reach zero
Collects one of them and keeps the other
js-advanced:5.explanation: V8 uses tracing (mark-and-sweep style) collection: anything not reachable from roots (stack, globals, handles) is garbage, cycles included. Leaking cycles is a problem of pure reference counting, which V8 doesn't use for JS objects.

js-advanced:5.prompt: You want to attach computed metadata to request objects you don't own, without stopping them from being garbage-collected after the request ends. What should you use?
options: A WeakMap keyed by the request object
A Map keyed by the request object
A plain object keyed by a request ID string
An array of [request, metadata] pairs
js-advanced:5.explanation: A WeakMap holds its keys weakly: once the request object is otherwise unreachable, the entry and its metadata can be collected. A Map, plain object or array keeps strong references and grows forever unless you remove entries yourself.

js-advanced:5.prompt: This function runs once per incoming request. Why does memory keep growing?
options: new Array(1e6) is always allocated outside the V8 heap
Arrays filled with strings can never be garbage-collected
The if check inside the interval makes a copy of `big` every second
Each setInterval is never cleared, so its closure keeps `big` alive forever
js-advanced:5.explanation: Active timers are GC roots. The interval callback closes over big, so every call adds another live interval holding a million-element array. Store the handle and clearInterval it when the work is done, or don't use an interval at all.

js-advanced:5.prompt: Why are lots of short-lived objects (temporary arrays and objects inside a request handler) relatively cheap for V8?
options: V8 reference-counts them and frees each one the moment it becomes unreachable
The garbage collector skips objects younger than one event-loop tick entirely
They die in the young generation, where a scavenger only copies the few survivors
V8 allocates them on the C++ stack, so they're freed as soon as the function returns
js-advanced:5.explanation: V8's heap is generational. New objects go into a small young space, collected by a scavenger whose cost scales with the surviving objects, not the dead ones. Objects that survive a couple of scavenges are promoted to old space, which uses the more expensive mark-sweep-compact.

js-advanced:5.prompt: Node prints 'MaxListenersExceededWarning: Possible EventEmitter memory leak detected. 11 close listeners added'. What's the most likely cause?
options: A close listener threw an error 11 times, so Node assumes its state is leaking
Code adds a listener to a long-lived emitter on every request and never removes it
More than 10 different EventEmitter instances exist in the process at the same time
One emitter fired the close event more than 10 times without anyone listening
js-advanced:5.explanation: The warning fires when one emitter has more than 10 listeners for the same event. The usual cause is calling .on() per request or per retry on a shared object (a socket, DB pool or process). Use once(), remove the listener when finished, or attach it a single time.

js-advanced:5.prompt: A batch job reads a 2 GB CSV with fs.readFileSync, splits it into lines and crashes with 'JavaScript heap out of memory'. What's the most robust fix?
options: Stream the file and process it line by line (e.g. a read stream with readline)
Increase --max-old-space-size to 8192 and rerun
Call global.gc() after splitting the file
Convert the whole file buffer to a string with toString('utf8') first
js-advanced:5.explanation: Reading the whole file, then building a giant string and an array of lines, needs several times the file size in memory. Streaming keeps memory flat regardless of file size. Raising the heap limit only moves the ceiling and fails again on the next bigger file.

js-advanced:5.prompt: Why shouldn't a FinalizationRegistry callback be used to close database connections or file handles?
options: FinalizationRegistry callbacks run synchronously inside the allocation that triggered GC
FinalizationRegistry only works with primitive values
Using it disables garbage collection for the registered objects
The callback may run much later or never, since GC timing isn't guaranteed
js-advanced:5.explanation: The spec makes no promise about when or whether cleanup callbacks run. They're for optional, best-effort cleanup. Resources need deterministic release: try/finally, an explicit close(), or `using` with Symbol.dispose.

js-advanced:5.prompt: Which of these commonly cause memory leaks in long-running Node servers? Select all that apply.
options: Adding a listener per request to a global emitter without removing it
Local variables inside a function that has already returned and isn't referenced by any closure
Two unreachable objects that reference each other
An unbounded in-memory cache (a Map that only ever grows)
setInterval timers that are never cleared
js-advanced:5.explanation: Leaks are unwanted reachability: caches, timers and listener arrays all keep data reachable from roots. Locals of a finished function with no surviving closure are collectable, and unreachable cycles are collected by V8's tracing GC.

js-advanced:5.prompt: Which statements about WeakMap are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Using an object as a key prevents that object from being garbage-collected
Primitive strings and numbers can't be used as keys
It can't be iterated and has no size property
A value stays alive as long as its key is reachable
js-advanced:5.explanation: WeakMap keys are held weakly, so they don't keep objects alive. Once a key becomes unreachable, its entry and value can go. Because entries can disappear at any GC, iteration and size aren't offered. Keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols), never strings or numbers.

js-advanced:5.prompt: A closure keeps the outer-scope variables it uses alive for as long as the closure itself is reachable.
options: True
False
js-advanced:5.explanation: That's how closures work, and it's the root of many leaks: a callback stored in a long-lived structure (timer, listener, cache) keeps everything it captured alive. Releasing the closure (clearing the timer, removing the listener) releases what it captured.

js-advanced:6.explanation: emit iterates a copy of the listener array. The once wrapper removes itself and then calls the handler, so after the first emit only the 'on' listener is left, and emit returns the remaining count (1). The second emit only reaches the 'on' listener.

This is the bug a naive emit has when it iterates the live listener array. a removes itself at index 0, so b shifts down to index 0, and forEach moves on to index 1, which no longer exists. b is skipped. Real emitters iterate a copy of the array.

distractors:
L1 e
L2 e
after emit

after emit
L1 e
L2 e
js-advanced:6.explanation: emit calls each listener synchronously. L1 logs right away; L2 only schedules a microtask. 'after emit' runs next on the same synchronous path, and the microtask runs once the current script finishes. Node's EventEmitter behaves the same way: synchronous dispatch.

js-advanced:6.prompt: In Node.js, when does a listener registered with emitter.on('data', fn) run after emitter.emit('data', x)?
options: Synchronously, inside the emit() call, in the order they were registered
On the next tick (process.nextTick), after the current function returns
In the next iteration of the event loop, during the poll phase
In parallel on a libuv thread-pool worker, so emit() returns at once
js-advanced:6.explanation: EventEmitter.emit calls every listener synchronously, in registration order, before returning. A listener that needs to defer work must schedule it itself (setImmediate, queueMicrotask). That's why a slow listener blocks the code that called emit().

js-advanced:6.prompt: A job runner does emitter.on('job', async (job) => { await process(job); }) and process() sometimes rejects. What happens to that rejection by default?
options: emit() awaits each async listener in turn and rethrows the error to whoever called emit()
EventEmitter always catches it and re-emits it as an 'error' event on the same emitter
The rejection is swallowed silently, because listeners' return values are discarded
It becomes an unhandled rejection, because emit() ignores the listener's returned promise
js-advanced:6.explanation: emit() calls listeners but ignores their return values, so the async listener's promise is dropped. In Node 15+ an unhandled rejection crashes the process by default. Catch inside the listener, or enable captureRejections so rejections are routed to the 'error' event.

js-advanced:6.prompt: What does await once(emitter, 'ready') (from node:events) resolve with?
options: The emitter itself, for chaining
undefined, since it only signals that the event happened
An array of the arguments passed to emit('ready', ...)
Only the first argument passed to emit('ready', ...)
js-advanced:6.explanation: events.once returns a Promise that resolves with an array of all the event's arguments (const [conn] = await once(server, 'connection')). It also rejects if the emitter emits 'error' while waiting, which makes it handy for startup code.

js-advanced:6.prompt: Code calls emitter.on('tick', () => update()) and later emitter.off('tick', () => update()), but the listener keeps firing. Why?
options: off() is asynchronous and the removal only takes effect on the next event-loop tick
The two arrow functions are different objects, so off() finds no matching listener
off() only removes listeners that were originally registered with once()
A listener can only be removed from inside its own callback, while it's running
js-advanced:6.explanation: Listeners are matched by reference. Each arrow-function expression creates a new function, so off() is given one that was never registered. Store the handler in a variable and pass that same reference to both on() and off().

js-advanced:6.prompt: A logging listener must run before listeners that other modules have already registered on the same emitter. Which Node EventEmitter method fits?
options: emitter.prependListener('event', fn)
emitter.on('event', fn) with a priority argument of 0
emitter.once('event', fn), since once-listeners always run first
emitter.setMaxListeners(0) before calling on()
js-advanced:6.explanation: prependListener (and prependOnceListener) inserts the listener at the front of the array, so it runs first. on() has no priority parameter, once() listeners run in registration order like any other, and setMaxListeners only changes the leak-warning threshold.

js-advanced:6.prompt: Which statements about Node's EventEmitter are correct? Select all that apply.
options: off(event, fn) removes every listener registered for that event
By default it warns when more than 10 listeners are added for a single event
emit() returns true if the event had listeners and false otherwise
Listeners are invoked asynchronously on the next tick
A once() listener is removed after its first call
js-advanced:6.explanation: The default maxListeners is 10 per event (a warning, not a hard limit). emit() returns a boolean and runs listeners synchronously. off/removeListener removes a single registration of that exact function; removeAllListeners(event) clears all of them.

js-advanced:6.prompt: You're writing your own minimal event emitter. Which are good implementation choices? Select all that apply.
options: Iterate over a copy of the listener array in emit()
Make off(event, fn) also work for handlers registered with once(), e.g. by storing the original fn on the wrapper
Store listeners in an object or Map of arrays keyed by event name
Call each listener through setTimeout so one slow listener can't block the others
Store listeners in a Set so registering the same function twice is ignored
js-advanced:6.explanation: Copying protects iteration against listeners that add or remove listeners. Mapping wrappers back to the original makes off() symmetric with once(). Wrapping in setTimeout changes the synchronous contract callers depend on, and a Set silently dedupes, which Node's emitter doesn't do.

js-advanced:6.prompt: Node's EventEmitter lets you add the same listener function more than once, and it is then called once per registration.
options: True
False
js-advanced:6.explanation: on() doesn't check for duplicates; each call appends another entry, so the function runs once per registration on each emit. removeListener removes only one entry at a time (the most recently added matching one).

js-advanced:7.explanation: Without an initial value, reduce uses the first element as the accumulator. On an empty array there's nothing to use, so it throws a TypeError. With a single element and no initial value, the callback never runs and that element (5) is returned. A correct polyfill has to copy all of these edge cases.

Native map skips holes in sparse arrays (it checks `i in arr`), so the callback runs twice. The result keeps the original length and keeps the hole, so index 1 doesn't exist in out. A naive polyfill that loops over every index would call the callback 3 times and write NaN at index 1.

Each call cancels the pending timer and starts a new one. log(2) replaces log(1)'s timer, and log(3) at about 5 ms replaces that one, so the only surviving timer fires around 25 ms. 'check' at 15 ms prints first, then 'fired 3'.

The JSON round-trip deep-copies but loses information. Dates become ISO strings, properties with undefined are dropped, NaN becomes null, and the nested object is a new copy. That's why structuredClone or a proper deepClone is preferred.

js-advanced:7.prompt: Why define a custom array helper with Object.defineProperty(Array.prototype, 'myMap', { value: fn, writable: true, configurable: true }) instead of Array.prototype.myMap = fn?
options: Plain assignment throws in strict mode, because Array.prototype is frozen by default
Plain assignment creates an enumerable property, so it shows up in for...in over arrays
Plain assignment only affects arrays created after the line runs, not existing ones
defineProperty makes the method faster, because V8 only inlines non-enumerable methods
js-advanced:7.explanation: Assigned properties are enumerable, so for...in loops over any array would visit 'myMap'. defineProperty defaults enumerable to false, matching native methods. Both forms affect existing arrays, because they share the prototype.

js-advanced:7.prompt: When writing a Promise polyfill, why must .then() callbacks always be queued as microtasks, even if the promise is already resolved?
options: So callbacks always run after the current synchronous code, whether or not it already settled
Because calling them synchronously would overflow the stack for any chain of two or more
Because the spec requires then() callbacks to run on a separate thread from the caller
So the garbage collector can detect unhandled rejections before the callbacks run
js-advanced:7.explanation: If then() ran callbacks synchronously for settled promises and asynchronously otherwise, the same code would sometimes run in a different order. Always deferring via queueMicrotask keeps behaviour predictable and matches native promises.

js-advanced:7.prompt: Which pairing of technique to use case is correct?
options: Throttle a search box's API call until typing pauses; debounce scroll handling to at most once every 100 ms
Debounce both, since throttle is just debounce with a shorter delay
Throttle both, since debounce can drop the final event
Debounce a search box's API call until typing pauses; throttle scroll handling to at most once every 100 ms
js-advanced:7.explanation: Debounce waits for a quiet period and fires once, which suits 'call after the user stops typing'. Throttle fires at most once per interval during continuous activity, which suits scroll or resize. Debounce keeps the last call, so it doesn't drop the final event.

js-advanced:7.prompt: In a reduce polyfill called without an initialValue, how should the accumulator be initialised?
options: With 0, starting the loop from index 0, since most reductions are sums
With an empty array, starting from index 0, so results can be collected
With the first present element, starting the loop from the next index
With undefined, starting the loop from index 0 so every element is visited
js-advanced:7.explanation: Native reduce uses the first existing element (skipping holes) as the accumulator and calls the callback from the following index, throwing a TypeError if the array is empty. Defaulting to 0 is wrong for string or object reductions.

js-advanced:7.prompt: Which bugs does this Promise.all polyfill have? Select all that apply.
options: It fails when an input is a plain value rather than a promise
Results come back in completion order instead of input order
It never settles when given an empty array
It rejects as soon as any input rejects
js-advanced:7.explanation: Using push stores values in completion order. Write results[i] = v and count completions instead. With [] no callback ever runs, so it never resolves; native Promise.all([]) resolves to []. Rejecting on the first rejection is correct, and Promise.resolve(p) already handles plain values.

js-advanced:7.prompt: Which statements about structuredClone() and JSON-based cloning are correct? Select all that apply.
options: structuredClone handles circular references
structuredClone throws when the value contains a function
structuredClone preserves class instances' prototypes and methods
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x)) preserves properties whose value is undefined
structuredClone copies Map, Set and Date objects correctly
js-advanced:7.explanation: structuredClone uses the structured clone algorithm: it supports Map, Set, Date, RegExp, typed arrays and cycles, and throws DataCloneError for functions. Class instances come back as plain objects without their prototype. The JSON round-trip drops undefined values entirely.

js-advanced:7.prompt: A correct debounce implementation must cancel (clear) the previously scheduled timer every time the debounced function is called.
options: True
False
js-advanced:7.explanation: Debounce means 'run only after N ms with no new calls'. Each call has to cancel the pending timer and schedule a new one; otherwise every call eventually fires and you've just delayed the calls instead of collapsing them.

js-advanced:8.prompt: In modern V8, what is Ignition's role?
options: It's the garbage collector that scavenges short-lived objects in the young generation
It's the optimizing compiler that turns hot functions into specialised machine code
It's the libuv component that runs the event loop and dispatches I/O callbacks
It's the interpreter: it generates bytecode, runs it and collects type feedback
js-advanced:8.explanation: V8 parses source into an AST, Ignition generates and interprets bytecode, and hot code is then compiled by higher tiers (Sparkplug, Maglev, TurboFan) using the type feedback Ignition gathered. Garbage collection is Orinoco, and the event loop belongs to libuv, not V8.

js-advanced:8.prompt: A hot function that has always received integers suddenly gets a string from a rare code path, and it briefly runs slower. What most likely happened?
options: V8 threw away all compiled code and recompiled the whole program from scratch
String arguments force V8 to run the function in a slower, sandboxed string-handling mode
V8 deoptimized it: the optimized code's type assumptions failed, so it fell back to a lower tier
The garbage collector promoted the function's code object to old space, which is slower to run
js-advanced:8.explanation: Optimizing compilers speculate based on observed types (e.g. 'a and b are always small integers'). When a guard fails, V8 deoptimizes, discarding the machine code and going back to a lower tier until it re-optimizes with broader assumptions. Keeping types consistent avoids this churn.

js-advanced:8.prompt: A utility reads obj.id from objects built in six different ways (different property orders and optional fields). What state does the inline cache at that property access most likely end up in?
options: Uninitialized: inline caches are disabled for objects with optional fields
Megamorphic: too many shapes, so V8 falls back to a slower generic lookup
Monomorphic: V8 merges all six shapes into one hidden class
Polymorphic with unlimited entries, so it stays just as fast
js-advanced:8.explanation: An inline cache handling one shape is monomorphic (fastest), a handful (up to about 4) is polymorphic, and beyond that it becomes megamorphic and uses a slower generic lookup. Building objects of the same 'type' in one consistent way keeps sites monomorphic.

js-advanced:8.prompt: Do a and b share the same hidden class (shape) in V8?
js-advanced:8.code:
const a = { x: 1, y: 2 };
const b = { y: 2, x: 1 };
options: No: the properties were added in a different order, so the shape transitions differ
Yes: they have exactly the same property names and the same value types
Yes: all object literals share one shape regardless of their keys and order
No: only objects created with a constructor or class get hidden classes at all
js-advanced:8.explanation: Shapes are built by transitions as properties are added, and order matters: {x, y} and {y, x} end up with different hidden classes. Code that sees both becomes polymorphic. Always creating objects with the same keys in the same order, e.g. via a factory or class, keeps them identical.

js-advanced:8.prompt: A hot path does delete session.tempToken on objects that are read heavily afterwards. What's the main performance concern, and the usual fix?
options: delete frees memory immediately, which triggers a full GC each time; batch the deletes instead
delete is asynchronous, so later reads race with it; await a microtask before reading again
delete copies the entire object into a new allocation; use Object.assign to remove keys instead
delete can push the object into slow dictionary mode; assign undefined or use a Map instead
js-advanced:8.explanation: Deleting properties (especially not the most recently added one) often turns a fast-shape object into a hash-table-backed dictionary object, which slows down every later access. Assigning undefined keeps the shape. For key sets that change at runtime, a Map is the right structure.

js-advanced:8.prompt: What does V8 mainly use to decide how to specialise a function when it optimizes it?
options: A static analysis pass that runs once on the whole program at startup
The order in which functions appear in the file
Type feedback collected by inline caches while the function ran in lower tiers
JSDoc and TypeScript type annotations in the source
js-advanced:8.explanation: V8 never sees TypeScript types; they're erased before runtime. Optimization is speculative, based on the shapes and types actually observed at each operation during execution, which is why a warm-up period matters and why changing types causes deopts.

js-advanced:8.prompt: Which statement about V8 array 'elements kinds' is correct?
options: Every array is stored as a hash table until it grows past 1,000 elements, then becomes packed
Transitions are one-way: once an array holds a double or string, it keeps the more general kind
V8 resets an array to its fastest kind as soon as all of its values are small integers again
Holes in arrays have no effect on how V8 stores the elements or how fast it accesses them
js-advanced:8.explanation: Arrays move from packed small integers to doubles to generic elements, and from packed to holey, but never back. Pushing 1.5 then 'x' into [1, 2, 3] leaves it in the generic kind for good. Creating sparse arrays (new Array(n) filled later) makes them holey and slower.

js-advanced:8.prompt: A cache adds and removes thousands of string keys per second. Which structure is the better fit for V8 performance and semantics?
options: A Map
A plain object with delete for removals
An array searched with findIndex
A frozen object recreated on every change
js-advanced:8.explanation: Map is designed for frequent insertion and deletion of arbitrary keys, keeps insertion order, has size, and has no prototype keys to collide with. Plain objects with heavy delete fall into dictionary mode and risk clashing with inherited names like 'constructor'.

js-advanced:8.prompt: Which coding habits help V8 generate fast code? Select all that apply.
options: Initialise all properties in the constructor, in the same order, for every instance
Call a hot function with consistent argument types
Delete properties frequently to keep objects small
Pre-allocate arrays with new Array(1000) and fill them sparsely
Avoid try/catch everywhere, because TurboFan never optimizes functions that contain it
js-advanced:8.explanation: Stable shapes and consistent types keep inline caches monomorphic and optimizations valid. Frequent delete and sparse (holey) arrays hurt performance. The try/catch rule is outdated: TurboFan has optimized functions containing try/catch for years.

js-advanced:8.prompt: Which statements about V8's role in Node.js are correct? Select all that apply.
options: V8 includes the garbage collector that manages the JS heap
V8 provides the event loop and async I/O
V8 compiles hot functions to optimized machine code
V8 implements the fs and net modules
Node uses V8 to parse, compile and execute JavaScript
js-advanced:8.explanation: V8 is the JS engine: compilation tiers, execution and the garbage-collected heap. The event loop, thread pool and async I/O come from libuv, and modules like fs and net are Node's own C++ and JS built on top of libuv.

js-advanced:8.prompt: Micro-benchmarks can be misleading because V8 may optimize away work whose result is never used.
options: True
False
js-advanced:8.explanation: Optimizing compilers do dead-code elimination, constant folding and inlining, so a loop computing a value nobody reads can shrink to almost nothing. Benchmarks should consume their results, warm up, and reflect realistic input shapes.

js-advanced:9.code:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0);
js-advanced:9.explanation: var is function-scoped, so all three callbacks share one i, which is 3 by the time they run. let creates a fresh binding for each loop iteration, so each callback captures its own j. Timers fire in the order they were scheduled.

Synchronous code runs first (1, 5). The microtask queue is then drained in FIFO order: the .then callback was queued before queueMicrotask, so 3 comes before 4. The timer is a macrotask and runs last.
Called as obj.getName(), this is obj. bind returns a function whose this is fixed permanently, and call, apply or another bind can't override it, so both later calls print 'bound'.

js-advanced:9.code: console.log([] == false, null == 0, null >= 0, NaN === NaN, Object.is(NaN, NaN));
js-advanced:9.explanation: [] == false converts both sides to numbers ('' then 0, and 0), giving true. null only loosely equals undefined, so null == 0 is false, but relational comparison converts null to 0, so null >= 0 is true. NaN is never === itself, while Object.is treats NaN as equal to NaN.

Function declarations are hoisted along with their body, so foo is already a function. var bar is hoisted but only assigned later, so it's undefined. let baz is hoisted into the temporal dead zone, and reading it before the declaration throws a ReferenceError.
Own-key order is: integer-like keys in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order, then symbols. Object.keys leaves out symbol keys entirely, so the result is 1,2,b,a.

An async function runs synchronously until its first await, so a1 prints before end. await null queues the rest of a() as a microtask before the .then callback is queued, so after the synchronous code finishes a2 prints, then p.

Writing index 10 extends length to 11 with holes. Setting length = 2 then truncates the array and deletes every element at index 2 and above, including index 10. So length is 2, arr[10] is undefined, and it serialises as [1,2].

js-advanced:9.prompt: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 evaluate to false in JavaScript, and what's the usual way to compare such values?
options: Results are rounded to 15 decimal places; call toFixed(20) on both sides before comparing
Binary doubles can't represent 0.1 exactly; compare within a tolerance such as Number.EPSILON
The + operator converts decimals to strings first; wrap both in Number() before adding them
=== compares boxed number objects by reference; use == so the values are compared instead
js-advanced:9.explanation: 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare within a tolerance or work in integer units (e.g. cents). == doesn't help, because both operands are already numbers.

js-advanced:9.prompt: Type coercion check: which of these comparisons are true? Select all that apply.
options: Number('') === 0
typeof null === 'object'
js-advanced:9.explanation: typeof null is 'object' (a historical bug). + with a string concatenates, giving '52', but - converts to numbers, giving 3. 0.1 * 3 is 0.30000000000000004. Number('') is 0, a common trap when parsing empty form fields.

js-advanced:9.prompt: const arr = []; arr.push(1); throws a TypeError because arr was declared with const.
options: True
False
js-advanced:9.explanation: const prevents rebinding the variable (arr = [] would throw), not mutating the value it points to. Pushing into a const array or changing a const object's properties is allowed. Use Object.freeze for shallow immutability.
